lead: Fault simulation asks how many listed faults a set of vectors catches. ATPG, automatic test pattern generation, asks the reverse: for one fault not yet caught, which input vector shows it at an output? The two programs work in a loop: fault simulation measures coverage, ATPG adds vectors for the faults still missed, and the loop stops at the coverage target. The compact vector set that comes out is applied to every chip that is made.
prereq: You need: the stuck-at fault list and collapsing from 6.2, and gate-level simulation from the Verilog chapters.

blocks.text: Fault simulation applies each vector to the good circuit and to every faulty circuit in the collapsed fault list. A fault is detected when at least one primary output differs between the good and the faulty circuit. A detected fault is dropped from the list, so later vectors simulate fewer faulty circuits (fault dropping).

A large chip has millions of faults, so speed matters. Serial simulation runs one faulty circuit at a time. Parallel simulation packs circuits into the bits of a machine word: a 32-bit word carries the good circuit in one bit and 31 faulty circuits in the others, and one bitwise AND evaluates a gate for all of them. Deductive simulation carries, on each line, the list of faults that would flip it. Concurrent simulation re-evaluates a faulty circuit only where it differs from the good one.

blocks.where: where FC is the fault coverage, 'detected' is the number of faults the vectors detect and 'total faults' is the size of the collapsed fault list.

blocks.text: Tools also report fault efficiency (some call it ATPG efficiency or test coverage): detected faults divided by the faults left after removing those ATPG proved redundant. It shows how well ATPG did on the faults that can be tested; fault coverage shows how well the chip is tested.

sections.h3: ATPG methods, from exhaustive to algorithmic

blocks.text: Exhaustive test applies all 2ⁿ vectors of an n-input circuit: complete, but impossible beyond small n. Pseudo-exhaustive test splits the circuit into small cones and exhausts each. Random test applies pseudo-random vectors and keeps those that detect new faults; weighted random biases the 0/1 probability of each input. Algorithmic ATPG works backwards from one target fault.

In the D-algorithm, D means 1 in the good circuit and 0 in the faulty circuit; D̄ means 0 in the good and 1 in the faulty circuit. The D-frontier is the set of gates with D or D̄ on an input and an output still unknown; the J-frontier is the set of gates whose output value is set but whose inputs are not yet justified.

items: Activate the fault: give the faulty line the opposite of its stuck value, creating D or D̄.

Propagate: pick a gate from the D-frontier and set its other inputs to non-controlling values (1 for AND/NAND, 0 for OR/NOR) so the difference passes through. Repeat until D or D̄ reaches a primary output.
Justify: work back from every value set so far to primary inputs, emptying the J-frontier.
Backtrack on a conflict: undo the last choice and try another. If every choice fails, the fault is redundant.

blocks.text: PODEM assigns values only at primary inputs, chosen by tracing back from the current objective, so its search space is the 2ⁿ input combinations rather than all internal lines and it usually backtracks less. FAN adds smarter backtracing through fanout-free regions and several objectives at once.

sections.h3: Redundant faults, compaction and the ATPG loop

blocks.text: A fault with no test is undetectable. In combinational logic an undetectable stuck-at fault is called redundant, because the line could be tied to that constant without changing the function. It comes from redundant logic, such as a consensus term added to remove a hazard, or from reconvergent fanout whose two paths cancel the difference. ATPG proves redundancy by exhausting the search; the designer may then remove the redundant logic, which also removes the fault.

Test compaction removes vectors that detect nothing new and merges vectors whose specified bits do not clash. Vector ordering puts high-yield vectors first so a bad chip fails, and leaves the tester, early. Neither changes the coverage of the final set.

The loop in the figure is iterative: simulate, check coverage, run ATPG on the undetected faults, add the new vectors, simulate again. It stops at the coverage target or when only redundant and aborted faults remain.

spec.aria: Three NAND gates computing Z equals A times B plus C, with A marked stuck at 0, B equal 1, C equal 0, G1 carrying D bar, G2 equal 1 and Z carrying D.

examples.question: The circuit is Z = A·(B + C), built as G1 = NAND(A, B), G2 = NAND(A, C), Z = NAND(G1, G2); input A fans out to both G1 and G2. Use the D-algorithm to find a test for A stuck-at-0. Show activation, the D-frontier at each step, propagation and the final vector, and give the good and faulty values of Z.
steps: Activate: A/0 needs A = 1 in the good circuit; the faulty circuit has A = 0. A carries D, and so do both fanout branches.
D-frontier = {G1, G2}: both gates have D on an input and an unknown output.
Propagate through G1: set B = 1 (non-controlling for NAND). Good G1 = NAND(1, 1) = 0, faulty G1 = NAND(0, 1) = 1, so G1 = D̄.
Set C = 0. Then G2 = 1 in both circuits, because a 0 input forces a NAND to 1. G2 leaves the D-frontier and becomes a steady 1 into the last gate.
D-frontier = {Z gate}. Z = NAND(D̄, 1): good NAND(0, 1) = 1, faulty NAND(1, 1) = 0, so Z = D and the difference has reached the output.
Justify: B = 1 and C = 0 are primary inputs, so the J-frontier is empty and no backtrack is needed. Vector ABC = 110.
examples.answer: ABC = 110 detects A stuck-at-0: Z = 1 in the good circuit and Z = 0 in the faulty circuit.

examples.question: For the same circuit, the collapsed fault list holds the eight checkpoint faults: A1/0, A1/1 (the branch of A into G1), A2/0, A2/1 (the branch into G2), B/0, B/1, C/0, C/1. Fault-simulate the vectors 110, 101, 011, 111, 100 in that order with fault dropping. Give the coverage after each vector and the compacted test set.
steps: For each vector find the good Z, then which remaining faults change Z.
Vector 111 is applied after 011; it would detect only faults already dropped, so it adds nothing.
examples.answer: Coverage climbs 25 %, 50 %, 75 %, 75 %, 100 %. Vector 111 detects nothing new and is removed, so the compacted set is {110, 101, 011, 100}: four vectors for 100 % of the eight faults.

traps: Reading D as 'fault present here'. D means good 1 and faulty 0; D̄ means good 0 and faulty 1.
Calling a vector a test because it activates the fault. It is a test only if a primary output differs.
Using the wrong denominator. Fault coverage divides by all faults in the list; fault efficiency leaves out the faults proved redundant.
Confusing the D-frontier (where the difference can move forward) with the J-frontier (values still to be justified backwards).
Thinking compaction or ordering raises coverage. They cut test time and tester memory; coverage stays the same.

quiz.q: Define D and D̄ in D-algorithm notation.
quiz.a: D is 1 in the good circuit and 0 in the faulty circuit. D̄ is 0 in the good circuit and 1 in the faulty circuit.

quiz.q: Write the formula for fault coverage and for fault efficiency.
quiz.a: FC = detected ÷ total faults × 100 %. Fault efficiency = detected ÷ (total faults − proven redundant faults) × 100 %.

quiz.q: How many faulty circuits does one 64-bit word carry in parallel fault simulation, and why?
quiz.a: 63. One bit is kept for the good circuit, so its values can be compared with the 63 faulty circuits in the other bits.

quiz.q: What is the job of the D-frontier and of the J-frontier during ATPG?
quiz.a: The D-frontier lists gates where the fault difference can be pushed one step towards an output. The J-frontier lists gates whose output has been fixed but whose inputs still have to be set from the primary inputs.

quiz.q: In the first worked example, find the test for B stuck-at-1 instead.
quiz.a: Activate: B = 0 (good 0, faulty 1, so B = D̄). Propagate through G1: A = 1, giving G1 = D. Block G2 from changing: with A = 1, G2 = NOT C, so set C = 0 to make G2 = 1. Then Z = NAND(D, 1) = D̄: good Z = 0, faulty Z = 1. Vector ABC = 100, matching the fault-simulation table.

quiz.q: A collapsed fault list has 4,000 faults. The vectors detect 3,600, and ATPG proves 160 of the rest redundant. Find FC and fault efficiency.
A vector detects no new fault in fault simulation with fault dropping. Should it be kept? Explain.
quiz.a: No. Every fault it detects was already detected by an earlier vector, so removing it loses no coverage and saves tester time. This is static compaction.

quiz.q: Why can 100 % fault coverage be impossible even for a correctly working design?
quiz.a: Some faults are redundant: no vector makes any output differ, because the logic is redundant or reconvergent paths cancel the difference. They stay in the fault list, so fault coverage stays below 100 % even when every testable fault is detected; fault efficiency can still reach 100 %.

beyond: Not for the exam. Commercial ATPG combines structural search with SAT solvers and runs fault simulation on many cores or GPUs. Cell-aware and layout-aware fault models add defects that classical stuck-at ATPG misses, and low-power ATPG fills don't-care bits to limit switching. Search 'SAT-based ATPG', 'X-filling' and 'cell-aware test'.
